Newly hatched Sooty tern chicks emerge at a remarkably consistent mass of 23.4 grams [Wwb = 23.4 grams], a value that positions them within the typical range for tropical terns whose semi-precocial young rely on rapid yolk absorption. The incubation period, a critical phase during which the embryonated egg develops at a mean temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], lasts approximately 28 days [ab = approximately 28 days] before the first feeding event occurs. This duration appears closely tied to the thermal regime within the nest, as slight deviations in microclimate can extend or shorten the developmental window. Once hatched, the downy chick is brooded almost continuously for its first few days, transitioning quickly from yolk dependence to parental provisioning. The energetic demands of this early stage are substantial, yet the initial body mass provides a sufficient buffer to sustain the nestling through the unpredictable feeding schedules that characterize pelagic foraging trips. Field measurements from Ascension Island colonies confirm that this neonatal weight is consistently observed across different breeding seasons, suggesting strong canalization of this particular life-history trait despite varying environmental conditions.

As the nestling progresses through its feather-growing phase, the ultimate wet weight of approximately 200 grams [Wwi = approximately 200 grams] is typically achieved just before fledging. This adult body mass represents a nearly tenfold increase from the hatching mass, reflecting the intensive provisioning effort undertaken by both parents during the brooded nestling stage. Under the typical thermal conditions of a tropical nesting colony (40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]), the time since birth at fledging is recorded at 56 days [tx = 56 days], a developmental schedule that aligns well with other Onychoprion species. During this period, the pin-feathered chick undergoes rapid wing feather elongation and begins to exercise its flight muscles in preparation for nest departure. The achievement of nutritional independence follows shortly after the first flight, although post-fledging dispersal may be gradual. Comparative data from the Dry Tortugas indicate that inter-colony variation in prey availability can shift the fledging age by several days, but the 56-day mark remains a reliable benchmark for populations with consistent food resources.

Sexual maturation in the Sooty tern does not occur immediately after fledging; instead, a protracted juvenile phase ensues. Under the same ambient thermal regime of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C] that characterizes the breeding season, the time since birth at puberty is approximately 168 days [tp = approximately 168 days]. This developmental milestone marks the onset of gonadal activity, though first reproduction is deferred considerably longer. The delay between achieving puberty and initiating breeding is thought to be linked to the time required for young birds to perfect foraging skills and accumulate adequate body condition. Field observations of first-year birds show that they often return to the natal colony but do not engage in courtship or nest building. Their plumage gradually transitions from the mottled juvenile pattern to the definitive adult coloration, a process that coincides with the hormonal changes associated with reproductive activation. This extended pre-breeding period is common among long-lived seabirds and may serve to reduce the cost of premature reproductive attempts.

The time since birth at first brood for the Sooty tern is estimated at 1,460 days [tR = 1,460 days] during the breeding season when ambient temperatures average 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This delayed onset of reproduction, roughly equivalent to four years of age, is a characteristic feature of a slow-paced life history strategy. During these pre-reproductive years, juveniles and subadults range widely across tropical and subtropical oceans, honing their ability to locate ephemeral prey patches. Once a bird commences breeding, it typically produces a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and most pairs raise only one brood per year [F_R_i = one brood per year], reflecting the energetic constraints of feeding a single nestling in an oligotrophic environment. The maximum reproductive rate is thus constrained by this low clutch size and annual frequency, as parents must invest heavily in the prolonged chick-rearing period. The consistency of single-egg clutches across the species' global range underscores the evolutionary stability of this reproductive strategy.

Maximum recorded longevity in the Sooty tern reaches approximately 13,067 days [am = approximately 13,067 days] when birds are active under the typical tropical body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This impressive lifespan, equivalent to nearly 36 years, places the species among the more long-lived members of the Laridae family and is consistent with the general pattern of high adult survival rates observed in tropical seabirds. Such extended longevity is a critical component of the species' demography, allowing individuals multiple breeding attempts over a lifetime despite the low annual productivity. Senescence appears to be gradual, with older breeders showing slightly reduced provisioning rates but maintaining comparable hatching success to prime-age adults. The physiological mechanisms underpinning this long lifespan likely include efficient antioxidant defenses and low basal metabolic rates relative to temperate congeners. Population modeling suggests that even small reductions in adult survival can have outsized impacts on population growth, highlighting the conservation significance of protecting adults from anthropogenic threats such as bycatch and introduced predators at nesting islands.
